cards.q: What does the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 require of an employer?
options: To remove every possible risk, whatever it costs
To ensure health and safety so far as reasonably practicable
Only to hand out personal protective equipment
Only to report accidents to the HSE afterwards
cards.why: Section 2: "so far as is reasonably practicable", weighing the risk against the cost and effort of reducing it.

cards.q: What do the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 (PUWER) cover?
options: Work equipment: suitable, maintained, inspected
Only brand new machines being sold
Only fixed electrical installations
Only cranes and other lifting equipment
cards.why: PUWER applies to the user of work equipment, new or old. The supply regulations apply to the maker selling it.

cards.q: A new machine is placed on the market in Great Britain. Which regulations does its maker have to meet?
options: PUWER 1998
The Electricity at Work Regulations 1989
COSHH 2002
The Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008
cards.why: They require the essential health and safety requirements, a technical file, a Declaration of Conformity and a UKCA mark (CE is also still accepted in Great Britain).

cards.q: Put ISO 12100's three steps of risk reduction in order.
cards.why: Design the hazard out first; guard what is left; only then warn and instruct. Each step covers what the one before could not.

cards.q: A risk is scored as severity × likelihood, each from 1 to 5. Severity is {s}. A new guard cuts the likelihood from {l1} to {l2}. By how many points does the score fall?
cards.why: Before: {s} × {l1}; after: {s} × {l2}. The severity is unchanged: a guard makes harm less likely, not less bad.

cards.q: ISO 12100 defines risk as a combination of what?
options: The cost of the machine and its speed
The number of hazards and of guards
The severity of harm and its probability
The operator's skill and their training
cards.why: Risk = severity × probability (the probability itself taking in exposure, the hazardous event and the chance of avoiding it).

cards.q: What is a RAMS?
options: A lock-off hasp for several padlocks
A risk assessment and method statement
A permit issued for hot work only
An accident and near-miss report form
cards.why: The risk assessment says what could go wrong and how it is controlled; the method statement, step by step, how the job is done safely.

cards.q: When is a permit to work used?
options: For high-risk jobs such as confined spaces
For every job on site, however small
Only for visitors to the site
Only for work in the offices
cards.why: A permit records the hazards, the isolations made, who may work and when it is handed back, for jobs where a mistake would be serious.

cards.q: Put the life of a permit to work in order.
items: Issuer checks hazards and makes the isolations
Worker reads and accepts the permit
Worker hands the permit back, work complete
Issuer checks, removes isolations and cancels it
cards.why: Nothing is switched back on until the work is handed back and the issuer has checked the area is clear.

cards.q: Under ISO 14120, what makes a fixed guard fixed?
options: It is welded on
It is interlocked to the machine
It is made of steel
It can only be removed with a tool
cards.why: A fixed guard needs a tool to remove; guards opened for routine access should be interlocked instead.

cards.q: When does an interlocked guard need guard locking (ISO 14119)?
options: Whenever the guard weighs more than 10 kg
Only on guards made of mesh or perforated sheet
When the machine stops slower than a person reaches it
Only while the machine is in manual mode
cards.why: If the hazard is still moving when a hand gets there, the guard must stay locked until it is safe to open.

cards.q: A light curtain with a detection capability of {d} mm guards a hazard. The whole system stops in {t} s. Using ISO 13855, $S = 2000T + 8(d - 14)$, how far from the hazard must it be, in mm?
cards.why: 2000 mm/s is the approach speed of a hand; the 8(d − 14) term allows for reaching through before a coarser curtain sees you. (If S comes out over 500 mm, the standard recalculates with 1600 mm/s.)

cards.q: What does Safe Torque Off (STO) do?
options: Isolates the drive from its incoming supply
Stops the drive making torque: the motor coasts
Brings the motor to a controlled, braked stop
Holds the motor still at standstill, under torque
cards.why: STO removes the energy that makes torque. It is not isolation: the drive and motor terminals stay live.

cards.q: What does Safe Stop 1 (SS1) do?
options: Brakes the motor under control, then applies STO
Applies STO at once
Limits the speed to a safe value
Stops the motor and keeps it held in position
cards.why: SS1 is stop category 1: a controlled stop, then torque removed. Category 0 (STO alone) lets the motor coast.

cards.q: What is Safely-Limited Speed (SLS) used for?
options: Making the axis run safely at its very top speed
Limiting the drive's output current to a safe value
Stopping the axis at a set, safe position each time
Letting an axis run slowly under watch, stopping it if too fast
cards.why: SLS monitors the speed against a safe limit, for setting or teaching with reduced risk, and triggers a safe stop if the limit is broken.

cards.q: In ISO 13849-1's risk graph, what sets the required performance level (PLr)?
options: The price of the machine and its options
How many safety relays the panel contains
Severity, exposure, and whether it can be avoided
The PLC's scan time and its memory size
cards.why: S (severity), F (frequency or duration of exposure) and P (possibility of avoiding it) lead to PLr a to e.

cards.q: What does Category 3 mean for a safety function's architecture?
options: It has no redundancy at all
One fault does not lose the safety function
Every fault is detected immediately
It must use a safety PLC
cards.why: Category 3: redundant channels, so one fault is tolerated, with reasonable fault detection. Category 4 also detects faults before they add up.

cards.q: A contactor's B10d is {b} operations. It switches {nop} times a year. What is its MTTFd, in years?
cards.why: ISO 13849-1: $MTTF_D = \frac{B_{10D}}{0.1 \times n_{op}}$, since B10d is when 10% have failed dangerously.

cards.q: What is a machine's technical file for?
options: Evidence it meets the requirements
The user's daily log book
The sales brochure and price list
The operators' training records
cards.why: The maker keeps it to show how the machine meets the essential requirements; the authorities can ask for it.

cards.q: Who signs a machine's Declaration of Conformity?
options: The customer's safety manager
An HSE inspector, after a visit
The installing electrician
The manufacturer or its representative
cards.why: By signing, the manufacturer takes legal responsibility that the machine complies.

cards.q: For how many years after the last machine of a type is made must its technical file be kept?
cards.why: Ten years, under the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008 (as under the EU Machinery Directive).
